samples.text:
In the past, parents and children spent a lot of time together, but nowadays many families do not do this. This essay will explain the causes of this situation and what can be done to improve it.

The first cause is work. In many families, both the father and the mother have full-time jobs, and they often come home late in the evening. When they arrive, they are tired and they still have to cook and clean, so there is not much time left for their children. Another cause is technology. Even when the family is at home together, each person is busy with their own phone, tablet or computer. For example, the children play online games in their room while the parents watch videos or check emails. Also, children today has many activities after school, like extra classes and sports training, so their timetable is very busy.

There are some things that can improve this situation. Firstly, families can make some simple rules, for example no phones during dinner time. This will give them chance to talk about their day. Secondly, parents can plan activities at the weekend which everybody enjoy, such as going to the park, cooking together or visiting relatives. Thirdly, companies could help by giving more flexible working hours, so parents can come home earlier and spend time with their kids.

In conclusion, parents and children spend less time together because of long working hours, technology and busy timetables. I think if families make some rules and plan activities together, and if companies are more flexible, the relationship between parents and children will become more closer.
samples.why: Causes and solutions both addressed with relevant, familiar ideas · limited development · mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly, Thirdly) · adequate but informal vocabulary (kids) · errors in agreement, articles and comparatives.

samples.text:
In many modern households, parents and children now share far less time together than previous generations did. This essay will examine the main reasons for this change and suggest some practical ways in which families could reconnect.

The most significant cause is the pressure of work. In many countries, it has become normal for both parents to work full-time, often with long commutes, and the expectation of being available by phone or email means that work frequently continues into the evening. As a result, parents may return home with little time or energy for their children. Children's own schedules have also become busier. Many attend extra tuition, sports clubs and music lessons after school, which leaves fewer free hours to spend with the family. Finally, digital technology has changed the way families use their time at home. Even when everyone is in the same room, each member may be absorbed in a separate screen, so being together physically does not necessarily mean interacting.

Improving the situation requires changes both inside and outside the home. Families could establish simple routines, such as eating at least one meal together each day without phones or television, which gives everyone a regular opportunity to talk. Parents might also consider reducing the number of organised activities their children attend, leaving space for unstructured time together at weekends. Employers have a part to play as well; flexible working hours and the option to work from home would allow parents to be present at key moments, such as after school. Shared hobbies, for example cycling or cooking, can also turn everyday tasks into chance for connection.

In conclusion, demanding jobs, busy schedules and technology have reduced family time. Through deliberate routines, a more balanced approach to children's activities and flexible employers, families can rebuild closer relationships.
samples.why: Clear focus on causes and solutions · each cause explained with its effect · solutions logically grouped inside and outside the home · good vocabulary (absorbed in, unstructured time) · one article slip.

samples.text:
Many parents today would readily admit that they spend less time with their children than their own parents spent with them. This shift is not the result of indifference but of economic, social and technological pressures, and while these cannot be removed entirely, families and employers can take practical steps to counteract them.

Economic demands are perhaps the most powerful cause. In many households, two incomes are now necessary to meet housing and living costs, and both parents may face long hours and lengthy commutes. The boundary between work and home has also blurred, as smartphones allow employers to reach staff at any time, so even evenings at home can be interrupted by messages and deadlines. Children's lives, meanwhile, have become increasingly scheduled. Parents anxious to give their children every advantage enrol them in tutoring, sport and music, leaving little unstructured time in which the family can simply be together. Technology intensifies the problem within the home itself: households in which each member retreats to a personal screen may be under one roof yet largely disconnected.

Addressing this requires deliberately protecting family time rather than expecting it to occur naturally. Simple, consistent rituals, such as a shared evening meal with devices set aside, create a daily space for conversation. Parents may also benefit from questioning whether every extracurricular activity is essential, since a less crowded timetable leaves room for the spontaneous moments that children often value most. Employers, however, hold considerable influence. Flexible hours, remote working and a culture that respects time off would allow parents to be present when it matters, such as at the end of the school day. Governments can reinforce this through adequate parental leave and protection against excessive working hours.

In conclusion, long working hours, overscheduled childhoods and pervasive technology have eroded family time. Protecting it depends on conscious choices at home, supported by workplaces and policies that value family life.
samples.why: Causes and solutions both fully developed and clearly linked · perceptive points (physically together yet disconnected) · well-managed cohesion · precise vocabulary (blurred, overscheduled, pervasive) · wide range of error-free structures.
